newsitem.title: UK: BOE says further UK rate rise likely to be needed.
newsitem.headline: BOE says further UK rate rise likely to be needed.

text.p: The Bank of England said a further increase in UK interest rates was likely to become necessary in due course as the government was unlikely to meet its 2.5 percent inflation target.

"Even after the recent increase in official interest rates of 1/4 percentage point, it remains more likely than not that inflation will be above the target at the end of the forecast horizon," it said in its quarterly Inflation Report.
"And the short-run rise in inflation means that there is now much less chance of inflation being below 2-1/2 percent during 1997. Achievement of the inflation target remains elusive."
The Bank's chief economist Mervyn King told a news conference it was possible that inflation could rise above 3.0 percent in the next month or so.
The inflation report said last week's rise in interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent should help to reinforce credibility.

"But what matters most is the continuous pursuit of a monetary policy which is consistent with achieving the target in the medium term. To ensure this outcome, some further rise in interest rates is likely to become necessary in due course."

The central bank noted that since its August inflation report, the short-run outlook for inflation had deteriorated, the effective exchange rate had risen by eight percent and GDP growth had been above trend in the third quarter.
The balance of the recovery had shifted from net exports to domestic demand, especially consumption, and that trend was likely to be reinforced by the rise of sterling.

"It would be a mistake, however, to try to alter the balance of the recovery by pursuing an easier monetary policy in order to offset the rise in the exchange rate. That would do nothing to control the growth of domestic demand."

"An appropriate fiscal policy can help to restrain the growth of either public or private consumption. But if monetary policy fails to counter-act the potential inflationary consequences of growth of domestic demand then, as in the late 1980s, the problem could become a weak rather than a strong exchange rate."
